theme: Bildad and Zophar intensify; Job’s redeemer confession
readingInstruction: Read Job 18:1-20:29. Bildad and Zophar both make speeches, and between them Job gives a speech in chapter 19 that contains the most famous words in the book. Read chapter 19 slowly, and read verses 23 to 27 aloud.
settingTheScene: This is the second cycle of speeches, and the friends are escalating. Bildad’s second speech is a chilling portrait of the fate of the wicked. Zophar’s is much the same. The emotional force behind their words is fear: if Job is innocent, then their whole picture of the world is broken. So they must make him guilty. In the middle comes Job’s answer, in which he is crushed, isolated, and accused, and out of the dark he says the thing for which the book is best known.
observation: Bildad says, “Is the earth to be forsaken for you, or the rock to be removed from its place?” (18:4).
He describes the wicked as trapped, terrified, and forgotten, and says, “He has no offspring or descendant among his people” (18:19).
Job answers, “How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words?” (19:2).
He says that God has wronged him and walled up his way (19:6-8).
Job’s family and friends have abandoned him, and even young children despise him (19:13-19).
“Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has struck me!” (19:21).
“Oh that my words were written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book! Oh that with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!” (19:23-24).
“For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth” (19:25).
“And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God, whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another” (19:26-27).
Zophar answers that the joy of the wicked is short (20:5), and that what they gain will be vomited up (20:15).
interpretation:
Bildad and Zophar use pictures that are meant to frighten. Their descriptions of the wicked person’s end are among the most vivid in the Bible. There is a light that goes out, a net that closes, terrors that chase him. But they are describing Job without saying his name. This is a kind of cruelty that wears the clothes of wisdom.

The speech Job gives in response is full of heartbreak. He lists everything he has lost in relationships: his brothers have estranged themselves, his close friends have forgotten him, his servants do not answer him, and his wife finds his breath strange. Even young boys despise him. To lose possessions is hard. To lose belonging is harder. Job begs his friends, “Have mercy on me.”

And then, out of this, comes the most astonishing section in the book. Job wishes that his words could be written down forever. He wants a permanent record, because he knows that his death will come before he has been vindicated. The words that follow are not a wish, though. They are a statement of certainty: “I know that my Redeemer lives.”

The Hebrew word for Redeemer is go’el, a legal term for the family member who rescues a relative in need: who buys back land lost to debt, who avenges a death, who protects the vulnerable. Job’s longing in chapter 9 for an arbiter and in chapter 16 for a witness has now become a conviction. He does not just hope for someone. He knows there is someone, and he calls that person a living Redeemer who “will stand upon the earth,” as though taking his place in a courtroom at the last.

And then the most daring part. “Yet in my flesh I shall see God.” Job expects to see God with his own eyes, after death, in his body. Whether he fully understood what he was saying is debated. But the words, set in the canon, carry a hope of bodily resurrection that is not fully revealed until the New Testament.

Notice that the verse is spoken from the lowest point of the book. Hope is not the fruit of good circumstances. It is a decision made in the dark.
connection: Boaz acts as a go’el in the book of Ruth, which you will read in Unit 8. Isaiah calls God Israel’s Redeemer many times (Isaiah 41:14; 43:14; 54:5). Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15:51-57 that the dead will be raised imperishable. Jesus says, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). Job’s hope is realized in the risen Christ.
application:
Memorize Job 19:25 this week. It is the unit’s theme verse. Say it aloud in the morning and at night.

Think about the Redeemer you have. What did Jesus do to buy you back, and what did it cost? Write a short paragraph about it.

If you have lost something in a relationship, say so honestly to God. Then ask him to hold the loss in his hand.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you believe about your Redeemer, in your own words.
Ask him to anchor you in that hope when loss surrounds you.
Thank Jesus for standing for you.
